# 052 · A max_stack that checks the depth only after a push, proved to find the deepest point

[← All examples](../README.md)

| Verdict | Categories | Severity if shipped | Change | Verified unit | Approach |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **✓ Verified: property holds on every input** | functional, performance, no-false-positive | none | refactor, behaviour change not intended | [`MaxStack#of`](../../examples/apps/mica/src/main/java/net/terminalvalue/mica/asm/MaxStack.java) | [B11: Property proofs](../../lib/README.md) |

> The assembler computes `max_stack` for a `Code` attribute: the deepest the operand stack gets, which for a straight-line sequence is the largest running sum of the instructions' stack effects. The loop compares the depth with the maximum after every instruction. A developer compares it only after an instruction that pushes more than it pops, since no other instruction can leave the stack deeper than it was. The property committed for the computation is the definition itself, `\max` over the prefix sums, written as nested JML quantifiers, under the assumption that the effects are those of JVM instructions. The prover checks the changed loop against it on every such sequence up to the bound; stated over every `int` effect instead, the same property refutes the change, on two effects whose sum wraps, which is the premise the developer's argument did not state.

## The change

Guard the comparison with the maximum by `delta[i] > 0`, so that the depth is compared only after an instruction with a positive stack effect; the comment says why that loses nothing. The tests for `max_stack` pass.

**Before** ([`MaxStack.java`](../../examples/apps/mica/src/main/java/net/terminalvalue/mica/asm/MaxStack.java), line 10):

```java

private MaxStack() {}

/** The {@code max_stack} of a straight-line sequence whose instructions change the depth by {@code delta}. */
public static int of(int[] delta) {
    int depth = 0;
    int max = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < delta.length; i++) {
        depth += delta[i];
        if (depth > max) {
            max = depth;
        }
    }
```

**After:**

```java

private MaxStack() {}

/**
 * The {@code max_stack} of a straight-line sequence whose instructions change the depth by {@code delta}. The
 * depth is compared with the maximum only after an instruction that pushes more than it pops; any other leaves
 * the stack no deeper than it was.
 */
public static int of(int[] delta) {
    int depth = 0;
    int max = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < delta.length; i++) {
        depth += delta[i];
        if (delta[i] > 0 && depth > max) {
            max = depth;
        }
    }
```

## What the verifier found

The method returns without throwing and `result == (\max int k; 0 <= k && k <= delta.length; (\sum int i; 0 <= i && i < k; delta[i]))` holds on every input where `(\forall int i; 0 <= i && i < delta.length; delta[i] >= -255 && delta[i] <= 2)` holds.

This is a proof over the whole domain (delta: int[] of length ≤ 8), not a sample. JBMC turned the statement into a satisfiability problem over the bytecode and showed that it has no solution: no input violates the property.

## Would the existing tests have caught it?

Every existing unit test passes, as it should (`java -ea net.terminalvalue.mica.Tests`, run against the patched code).

## Why it matters

The argument is short and the places where such arguments break are the ends, the zeros and the premises nobody wrote down: an empty sequence, a sequence that only pops, an instruction with effect 0, the maximum reached on the last instruction, and a depth that is an `int`. A `max_stack` one too small is rejected by the type checker at class load, on the first method that reaches the depth; a `max_stack` one too large is accepted and costs a slot. The tests cover an addition, a pair of longs, an empty method and a sequence whose deepest point is not its last.

## Why the verdict is right

The property committed for `of` is the definition of `max_stack` from JVMS §4.7.3 for a straight-line sequence, in JML: `result == (\max int k; 0 <= k && k <= delta.length; (\sum int i; 0 <= i && i < k; delta[i]))`, the largest prefix sum, the empty prefix included so that a sequence that only pops has `max_stack` 0. The tool compiles the nested quantifiers to nested loops in the generated harness, one folding a maximum over the other's sums, and JBMC proves the changed loop against it on every sequence of up to eight effects in the range of JVM instructions, -255 to 2, which the property assumes: an invoke pops at most the 255 slots a descriptor may take, and nothing pushes more than two. That assumption was not in the first draft of the property, and without it the prover refuted the change in a second, on a sequence of two effects, shrunk from the seven the solver gave: two large negative numbers whose sum wraps below `Integer.MIN_VALUE`, so that the depth jumps to `Integer.MAX_VALUE` on a pop, which the original loop records and the changed loop, having seen a pop, does not. The developer's argument, that a pop cannot deepen the stack, is true of a stack and false of an `int`, and the proof found the premise. The assumption that makes it true is the one a JVM provides, it is on the page as part of the property, and the change is accepted under it because the specification holds of it, not because the old loop and the new one agree.

## What to do

Merge, with the assumption. The definition stays as the property and the range of the effects as its premise; the next change to the loop, say one that tracks the depth in a `short`, is checked against both the same way.

## Evidence

How the verdict was reached: JBMC 6.11.0: 5 properties proved over delta: int[] of length ≤ 8 in 30.5 s; loops unwound 16 times with unwinding assertions.

/** Generated by jvmcontract: asserts a property of a method on every input. The class file JBMC checks is generated directly; this is the same statement, for readers. */
/* \forall, \exists, \sum, \num_of, \max and \min are JML's quantifiers; the class file evaluates each as a loop over its range. */
public final class PropertyHarness {
    public static void check(int[] delta) {
        if (!((\forall int i; 0 <= i && i < delta.length; delta[i] >= -255 && delta[i] <= 2))) { return; } // the inputs the property is about
        int result = 0;
        int e = 0;
        try { result = net.terminalvalue.mica.asm.MaxStack.of(delta); } catch (java.lang.NumberFormatException t) { e = 1; } catch (java.lang.ArithmeticException t) { e = 2; } catch (java.lang.NullPointerException t) { e = 3; } catch (java.lang.ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException t) { e = 4; } catch (java.lang.StringIndexOutOfBoundsException t) { e = 5; } catch (java.lang.IndexOutOfBoundsException t) { e = 6; } catch (java.lang.NegativeArraySizeException t) { e = 7; } catch (java.lang.ClassCastException t) { e = 8; } catch (java.lang.IllegalStateException t) { e = 9; } catch (java.lang.IllegalArgumentException t) { e = 10; } catch (java.lang.UnsupportedOperationException t) { e = 11; } catch (java.util.NoSuchElementException t) { e = 12; } catch (java.util.ConcurrentModificationException t) { e = 13; } catch (java.lang.RuntimeException t) { e = 14; } catch (java.lang.Error t) { e = 15; }
        assert e == 0 && (result == (\max int k; 0 <= k && k <= delta.length; (\sum int i; 0 <= i && i < k; delta[i]))); // no exception, and the property

}
